posts.text:
Monroe County, Ohio. About 5:30 in the morning, in an account published September 26, 2026.

A coal miner is driving home from the night shift in southeastern Ohio when he notices something large crouched in the road ahead of him. It has bright, glowing red eyes, and they look directly at him. Very large wings are wrapped around its body as it crouches there. He has never seen anything like it in his life.

He drives past it. When he looks behind him, it is simply gone. He never saw it take off or leave.

His son hears the story on a phone call. His father tells him it happened the previous week, and his voice is shaky in a way the son has never heard before. The father is normally a skeptic, and he will not even say which road it was, because he believes his son would go out and investigate. He had never heard the name Mothman. People who heard his story gave it that name afterward.

The son sent the account to Phantoms & Monsters, which notes there is no exact date, no named witness, no exact location, and no image, and that an animal misidentification or a misleading visual impression is still possible. The son writes that he hopes the old idea about these sightings bringing bad luck isn't true. Still, a miner says that one morning around 5:30, something with red eyes looked straight at him from the road.

Source: https://deadofnightdispatch.com/dispatches/monroe-county-ohio-mothman-coal-miner-red-eyes-road/
posts.headline: Monroe County, Ohio. About 5:30 in the morning, in an account published September 26, 2026.

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Voynich manuscript?

Top 5 things to know about the unreadable book:

1) The Voynich manuscript is an illustrated codex written in an undeciphered script nicknamed Voynichese, with fantastical plants, bathing figures, and astrological diagrams on most pages.

2) University of Arizona radiocarbon dating of the calfskin parchment puts it between 1404 and 1438, and stylistic clues point toward an Italian Renaissance origin even though the text remains unread.

3) It is named for Polish book dealer Wilfrid Voynich, who bought it in 1912; the first confirmed earlier owner was Prague alchemist Georg Baresch in the seventeenth century.

4) American and British codebreakers including William and Elizebeth Friedman studied it without success, and no proposed decipherment has been independently verified.

5) Since 1969 it has lived at Yale's Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, which published the entire manuscript online in 2020, keeping the world's most famous unread book in public view.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voynich_manuscript
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Voynich manuscript?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Nazca lines?

Top 5 things to know about Peru's desert geoglyphs:

1) The Nazca lines are geoglyphs etched into the Nazca Desert of southern Peru between about 500 BC and 500 AD by removing reddish pebbles to expose lighter soil underneath.

2) Most are straight lines and geometric shapes, but more than seventy are animals and plants, including a hummingbird, monkey, spider, condor, and a human figure, some hundreds of meters long.

3) Together the lines run more than 1,300 kilometers and cover about fifty square kilometers on the dry, windless plateau between Nazca and Palpa, which is why so many have survived.

4) Peruvian archaeologist Toribio Mejia Xesspe spotted them while hiking in 1927, and American historian Paul Kosok, flying over in 1940 to 1941, realized one design was a bird and linked others to solstice alignments.

5) Scholars generally give them religious meaning rather than landing-strip fantasies, and UNESCO named the lines a World Heritage Site in 1994; drones keep finding hundreds of new figures.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazca_lines
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Nazca lines?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the dybbuk?

Top 5 things to know about Judaism's clinging spirit:

1) In Jewish mythology a dybbuk is a malicious possessing spirit understood as the dislocated soul of a dead person, from the Hebrew root meaning to adhere or cling.

2) The term appears in sixteenth-century writings and was popularized for wider audiences by S. An-sky's 1920 Yiddish play The Dybbuk, later filmed in 1937 as a classic of Yiddish cinema.

3) Early modern accounts cluster in kabbalistic Safed and Ottoman Galilee, where doctrines of gilgul, the transmigration of souls, gave rabbis a framework for why a restless dead soul might enter the living.

4) Traditionally the spirit was said to leave once it finished its task or was exorcised, and possession narratives often involved confession, unfinished guilt, or family conflict as much as supernatural terror.

5) Modern cases still surface and remain contested, including a widely televised 1999 exorcism in Dimona, Israel, while other rabbinic voices insist many claims belong to psychiatry rather than ritual.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dybbuk
posts.headline: Have you heard of the dybbuk?

posts.text:
Have you heard of crop circles?

Top 5 things to know about the flattened-field mystery:

1) A crop circle is a pattern made by flattening cereal crops, usually wheat or barley, and the term itself was coined in the early 1980s as reports surged in southern England.

2) Fringe theories have blamed aliens or obscure natural forces, but physicists note that published circles fall within the range of human hoaxing, and no scientific evidence supports exotic causes.

3) In 1991, Doug Bower and Dave Chorley publicly took credit for making more than two hundred English crop circles with planks, rope, and a baseball cap fitted with a loop of wire as a sight.

4) After their interviews, the number of reported formations jumped, and circles in Britain tend to appear near roads and areas of medium to high population rather than randomly across remote land.

5) Earlier odd flattened patches exist in the record, including the 1966 Tully "saucer nest" in Australia, but the classic pictogram boom is a late-twentieth-century media and hoax phenomenon.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crop_circle
posts.headline: Have you heard of crop circles?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the foo fighters?

Top 5 things to know about the WWII mystery lights:

1) Allied night-fighter pilots in World War II used "foo fighters" for unidentified glowing objects that paced their aircraft over Europe and the Pacific, with formal reports clustering from November 1944 onward.

2) The name stuck after radar operator Donald J. Meiers of the U.S. 415th Night Fighter Squadron borrowed "foo" from the Smokey Stover comic strip during a November 27, 1944 debriefing at their base near Dijon, France.

3) Crews described fiery balls of red, white, or orange light that made wild turns, flew in formation with planes, and vanished, yet never opened fire, leading many to assume a secret enemy weapon.

4) Similar sightings were later acknowledged among German and Japanese pilots as well, undercutting the simple idea that only one side was testing a new device.

5) After the war the Robertson Panel floated explanations such as St. Elmo's fire, electromagnetic effects, or light reflecting from ice crystals, but the wartime reports remain a foundational chapter of modern UFO lore.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foo_fighter
posts.headline: Have you heard of the foo fighters?

posts.text:
Answer: D) Inkanyamba

The Inkanyamba is a legendary serpent of South African Zulu and Xhosa folklore, said to dwell especially in the deep pool at Howick Falls on the Umgeni River in KwaZulu-Natal, where locals nickname it Howie. Tellings cast it as a huge serpentine dragon or storm spirit whose coiling body can stretch from water to sky, often with a horse-like or dragon-like head, sometimes fins, wings, or horns. Summer storms and tornadoes are blamed on its anger, and contact is said to be deadly.

How'd you do?
posts.headline: Answer: D) Inkanyamba

posts.text:
East of Marfa, Texas, on the high Chihuahuan Desert. First written account in 1883.

Young cowhand Robert Reed Ellison is driving cattle through Paisano Pass when he sees a flickering light and wonders if it is an Apache campfire. Other settlers say they have seen the same lights and found no ashes when they rode out. Joe and Anne Humphreys report them again in 1885. The first magazine write-up lands in Coronet in July 1957.

Modern skywatchers gather at a roadside viewing area about nine miles east of town on U.S. 90, looking south-southwest toward Chinati Peak and Mitchell Flat. Witnesses describe orbs that change intensity and color, usually yellow-orange but sometimes green, blue, or red, hovering above desert scrub, splitting, merging, or drifting where ranch lights do not belong.

A University of Texas at Dallas student team in May 2004 timed lights against traffic on Highway 67 and concluded the ones they recorded were car headlights distorted by desert air. Other researchers still log unexplained nights. The lights remain Marfa's signature mystery, half tourist draw and half unanswered desert file.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marfa_lights
posts.headline: East of Marfa, Texas, on the high Chihuahuan Desert. First written account in 1883.

posts.text:
Hill of Tepeyac, outside what is now Mexico City. December 1531.

According to the Nican Mopohua, Juan Diego, a Chichimec peasant, sees a young woman on Tepeyac who speaks Nahuatl and identifies herself as Mary, mother of the true deity. She asks for a church on that hill. Archbishop Juan de Zumárraga does not believe him and demands a miraculous sign.

On December 12, after the Virgin intercepts Juan Diego on his way to find a priest for his dying uncle, she tells him to gather flowers from the barren, freezing summit. He finds Castile roses, not native to Mexico, blooming there. She arranges them in his tilma. When he opens the cloak before Zumárraga, the roses fall and an image of the Virgin appears on the fabric.

The next day his uncle Juan Bernardino is well and says he also saw her, and that she wished to be known as Guadalupe. The tilma is installed in a chapel on Tepeyac by December 26. Today it hangs in the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe, the most-visited Catholic shrine in the world.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Our_Lady_of_Guadalupe
posts.headline: Hill of Tepeyac, outside what is now Mexico City. December 1531.

posts.text:
St. Francisville, Louisiana. The Myrtles Plantation, built in 1796.

The antebellum house sits behind a 125-foot veranda of ornamental cast iron and is now a bed and breakfast famous for ghost tourism. In 1948 Clarence John Laughlin noted its haunted presence in Ghosts Along the Mississippi. By the 1980s the National Enquirer had dubbed it America's Most Haunted House, and guidebooks still give it more entries than almost any other plantation.

The only verified murder in the house is that of William Drew Winter, shot on the front porch. Legend says he staggered or crawled up the main staircase and collapsed on the seventeenth step, and visitors still report a presence that stops there. A mirror in the house is said to hold the spirits of Sara Woodruff and two of her children, overlooked when mirrors should have been covered after a death, with handprints sometimes claimed on the glass.

The most told story is of Chloe, an enslaved woman in a green turban who supposedly poisoned a birthday cake with oleander. Historians note there is no record of a slave named Chloe, and Sara and her children died of yellow fever, not poison. Still, the Mystery Tours run nightly, and the house has been filmed for Unsolved Mysteries, Ghost Hunters, Ghost Adventures, and a 2024 Netflix Files of the Unexplained episode.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myrtles_Plantation
posts.headline: St. Francisville, Louisiana. The Myrtles Plantation, built in 1796.

posts.text:
Burke, Fairfax County, Virginia. October 1970.

On the night of October 19, U.S. Air Force Academy cadet Robert Bennett and his fiancée are parked in a field on Guinea Road when something moves outside the rear window. A man in a white suit with long bunny ears runs from the bushes, shouts that they are on private property, and throws a hatchet through the passenger window. They flee uninjured. The hatchet is still on the floorboard when police arrive. His fiancée remembers a white hood more than ears, but both say they saw his face clearly in the dark.

Ten days later, on Halloween night, construction security guard Paul Phillips finds a man in a gray, black, and white bunny costume on the porch of an unfinished house in Kings Park West on Guinea Road. Phillips puts him at about twenty years old, five foot eight, and one hundred seventy-five pounds. When Phillips speaks, the man starts chopping a porch post with a long-handled axe, then warns that trespassers will lose their heads. Phillips goes for his handgun. By the time he returns, the figure has run into the woods.

Fairfax County Public Library historian Brian A. Conley later ties both reports to the Bunny Man legend. Most later versions move the story to Colchester Overpass near Clifton, the Southern Railway span locals call Bunny Man Bridge.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunny_Man
posts.headline: Burke, Fairfax County, Virginia. October 1970.

posts.text:
Chicago O'Hare International Airport. Afternoon of November 7, 2006.

Around 4:15 p.m., a United Airlines ramp worker pushing back Flight 446 for Charlotte looks up and sees a dark gray metallic disc hovering over Gate C-17. He radios the crew. Within minutes, about a dozen United employees, including pilots, managers, and mechanics, are outside watching a silent saucer estimated between six and twenty-four feet across.

No air traffic controllers see it. Radar does not paint it. Several people outside the airport also report a disc over the field. One witness says it shoots straight up through the cloud deck and leaves a clean blue hole that closes behind it. The object is visible for roughly five minutes.

United Airlines and the FAA first say they have nothing. After the Chicago Tribune files a FOIA request, an internal review finds a United supervisor's call to the tower about the UFO. The FAA calls it a weather phenomenon, possibly a hole-punch cloud, and declines to investigate further. Witnesses remain upset that one of the world's busiest airports brushed off a craft hovering in plain sight over an active gate.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_O'Hare_International_Airport_UFO_sighting
posts.headline: Chicago O'Hare International Airport. Afternoon of November 7, 2006.

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Tower of Babel?

Top 5 things to know about the tower that scattered the languages:

1) The Tower of Babel story in Genesis 11 is an origin myth meant to explain why the world has many languages and cultures, though the Bible itself never uses the exact phrase "Tower of Babel."

2) In the account, a united human race speaking one language settles in Shinar, Lower Mesopotamia, and sets out to build a city and a tower that will reach the sky.

3) Yahweh sees their unity and power, confounds their speech so they can no longer understand one another, and scatters them across the earth, leaving the city unfinished.

4) The Hebrew name Babel is linked in the story to the verb balal, "to jumble or confuse," a wordplay on the name of Babylon, whose Akkadian name Bab-ilim meant "gate of God."

5) Modern scholars often connect the tale to real Mesopotamian ziggurats, especially Etemenanki, the great temple tower of Marduk in Babylon, and a related confusion-of-tongues theme appears in the older Sumerian story Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_Babel
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Tower of Babel?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Mary Celeste?

Top 5 things to know about the most famous ghost ship:

1) Mary Celeste was a Canadian-built, American-registered merchant brigantine found adrift and deserted in the Atlantic Ocean off the Azores on December 4, 1872, by the brigantine Dei Gratia.

2) The ship was in a dishevelled but seaworthy condition under partial sail, with its lifeboat missing, and the last log entry was dated ten days earlier.

3) She had left New York City for Genoa on November 7 with a cargo of alcohol that was still intact when found, and the captain's and crew's personal belongings were undisturbed.

4) None of the people who had been on board were ever seen or heard from again, and the salvage hearings that followed in Gibraltar only deepened the mystery.

5) Built in Spencers Island, Nova Scotia, and launched in 1861 as Amazon before being renamed under American ownership in 1868, Mary Celeste had sailed uneventfully until that 1872 voyage that made her name a byword for unexplained disappearance.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Celeste
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Mary Celeste?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Cottingley Fairies?

Top 5 things to know about the fairy photographs that fooled a nation:

1) The Cottingley Fairies appear in five photographs taken in 1917 by cousins Elsie Wright, then 16, and Frances Griffiths, then 9, beside a beck behind the family house in Cottingley, near Bradford, England.

2) The first plate showed Frances behind a bush with four fairies dancing in front of her, and a later shot showed Elsie on the lawn holding out her hand to a gnome about a foot tall.

3) Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, creator of Sherlock Holmes, used the pictures to illustrate a fairy article in the Christmas 1920 Strand Magazine and treated them as clear evidence of the supernatural.

4) Elsie's father, an amateur photographer, dismissed the figures as cardboard cutouts from the start, but public fascination lasted for decades after interest first faded in the early 1920s.

5) In the early 1980s both women admitted the photographs were faked with cardboard cutouts copied from a children's book, though Frances still maintained that the fifth and final photograph was genuine, and the photos and cameras are now held by the National Science and Media Museum in Bradford.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cottingley_Fairies
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Cottingley Fairies?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Battle of Los Angeles?

Top 5 things to know about the Great Los Angeles Air Raid of 1942:

1) The Battle of Los Angeles is the name newspapers gave to a rumored Japanese air attack and the anti-aircraft barrage that lit up the sky over Los Angeles from late February 24 into early February 25, 1942.

2) It came less than three months after Pearl Harbor and one day after a Japanese submarine shelled Ellwood near Santa Barbara, when West Coast cities were already running blackouts and bracing for invasion.

3) Gunners poured anti-aircraft fire into the night. Five civilians died during the barrage, and four Japanese aircraft were erroneously reported shot down, though no enemy planes were ever confirmed.

4) Secretary of the Navy Frank Knox called the episode a "false alarm" soon afterward, while some newspapers speculated about a cover-up to hide a real raid.

5) Later official histories pointed to a meteorological balloon sent aloft around 1:00 am as the trigger, with war nerves, stray flares and shell bursts from neighboring batteries feeding the chaos, and the U.S. Office of Air Force History in 1983 summed it up as war nerves sparked by a lost weather balloon.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Los_Angeles
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Battle of Los Angeles?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Shroud of Turin?

Top 5 things to know about the cloth some believe wrapped Jesus:

1) The Shroud of Turin is a length of linen bearing a faint image of the front and back of a naked man, with details that match traditional depictions of Jesus after crucifixion, and it has been venerated for centuries especially in the Catholic Church.

2) The image is clearer in photographic negative, a fact that drew worldwide attention after Secondo Pia photographed the shroud in 1898 and saw a lifelike positive face appear on his negative plate.

3) In 1988, radiocarbon dating by three independent laboratories dated samples of the cloth to the Middle Ages, between 1260 and 1390, a result most experts accept even as public debate continues.

4) Forensic microscopist Walter McCrone, examining adhesive-tape samples taken in 1978, argued the image was painted with red ochre in a gelatin medium and that the apparent bloodstains were vermilion pigment, findings other researchers dispute.

5) Defenders of authenticity often argue the tested samples were contaminated or taken from a medieval repair, but those fringe theories have been rejected by most experts, and the nature of the image remains contested in both scholarly literature and the popular press.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shroud_of_Turin
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Shroud of Turin?

posts.text:
Answer: C) Squonk

The squonk is a mythical creature said to live in the hemlock forests of northern Pennsylvania. The earliest written account appears in the 1910 book Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods, which describes a shy, always-unhappy animal with loose warty skin that weeps constantly, leaving a tear-stained trail hunters can follow. When cornered or badly frightened, the story goes, it may dissolve itself entirely in its own tears. Its mock scientific name, Lacrimacorpus dissolvens, is Latin for a body that dissolves in tears, and Johnstown, Pennsylvania, still celebrates it each August at Squonkapalooza.

How'd you do?
posts.headline: Answer: C) Squonk

posts.text:
Fatima, Portugal. October 13, 1917.

Tens of thousands of people crowd the Cova da Iria after three shepherd children, Lucia Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, say the Virgin Mary promised a miracle on this date so that all may believe. It has been raining. The ground is mud.

Then, according to scores of witnesses, the clouds break. The Sun appears as an opaque, spinning disc, duller than usual, throwing multicolored light across the landscape, the crowd and the clouds. Many say it careens toward the Earth before zig-zagging back into place. The event lasts about ten minutes. Some report that their soaked clothes and the muddy ground dry suddenly. Not everyone sees the same thing. Some see only the colors. Some see the Lady. Some see nothing at all. Crowd estimates run from about 50,000 to about 70,000.

Secular reporters and officials are among those who describe the solar display. The local bishop opens a canonical investigation that November, and on October 13, 1930, Bishop Jose da Silva declares the miracle worthy of belief. Critics later argue the accounts are inconsistent and that staring at the Sun can trick the eyes. Believers still call it the Miracle of the Sun.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miracle_of_the_Sun
posts.headline: Fatima, Portugal. October 13, 1917.

posts.text:
Darien, Georgia, near the mouth of the Altamaha River. 1981.

Former newspaper publisher Larry Gwin is fishing with his friend Steven Wilson in the coastal marshes when something big moves in the water. They say it shows two humps about five feet apart and leaves a wake like a speedboat. Newspapers across the country pick up the story, and other witnesses start talking.

Harvey Blackman of Brunswick says he saw it in the 1970s at a spot called Two Way on the Altamaha, a snake-like head on a body fifteen to twenty feet long. Frank Culpepper reports a wake so large it bounced the boats, and one of his companions ran for a rifle before the thing was gone. Believers describe an animal up to about thirty feet long with flippers like a seal.

People have been telling versions of this for a long time. In April 1830, Captain Delano of the schooner Eagle reported a creature about seventy feet long off St. Simons Island, alligator-shaped head raised about eight feet out of the water, and other men on the schooner backed him up. Darien itself was founded by Scottish Highlanders from the Inverness country around Loch Ness. Locals just call the modern beast the Altamaha-ha, or Altie.

Source: https://www.exploresouthernhistory.com/altamahaha.html
posts.headline: Darien, Georgia, near the mouth of the Altamaha River. 1981.

posts.text:
San Jose, California. 1886 to 1922.

Sarah Winchester, widow of the Winchester rifle fortune, buys a two-story farmhouse on forty-five acres near San Jose and starts expanding it herself. Room by room. Stairways that rise only a few feet. Doors and windows that end up sealed inside new walls. A seven-story tower torn down and rebuilt again and again. By the time she dies on September 7, 1922, the place is a maze.

Nine months later it opens as a tourist attraction. The stories grow with the house. A popular telling, traced by historians to a 1967 book, says Sarah visited a Boston medium who told her the ghosts of people killed by Winchester rifles were on her, and that she must build a house for them and never finish it. Researchers have found no solid evidence she met that medium, but the legend stuck to the brochures.

Today visitors and guides still report cold spots, footsteps, cooking smells, whispering, doors slamming on their own, and the feeling of being watched. Skeptic Joe Nickell chalks it up to suggestion and a drafty Victorian labyrinth. Believers call it one of America's most haunted houses. Either way, the halls keep turning, and the doors still lead nowhere.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester_Mystery_House
posts.headline: San Jose, California. 1886 to 1922.

posts.text:
Colorado. October 1, 2023.

A local law enforcement officer in Colorado looks up and starts filming. What he sees, he later calls an orb. Silent. Red, blue and green lights flashing. He puts it at about 300 feet off the ground. A radar check, he says, shows no aircraft in the area.

According to a redacted transcript later released with the case, the object hangs there for about fifteen minutes, then starts to fly closer. The exact town name is blacked out in the public file.

On September 18, 2026, the Pentagon's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office publishes the material as PURSUE Release 06: four cellphone clips from that same night, plus the one-page transcript. Parts of the videos are blurred at the bottom to protect privacy. Officials note the footage came from a cellular device, and that autofocus and image processing can distort distant subjects.

AARO has not identified the object. The case remains unresolved. No claim of exotic technology appears in the official record. Just a silent, multicolored orb on a Colorado night, recorded by a cop, and still unexplained years later.

Source: https://www.denvergazette.com/2026/09/22/feds-share-video-of-uap-that-was-captured-by-law-enforcement-in-colorado/
posts.headline: Colorado. October 1, 2023.

posts.text:
Near Winona, Minnesota. Late 1960s.

In a refrigerated glass coffin on a private property near Winona, carnival promoter Frank Hansen is touring something he bills as the missing link. Inside the ice is a hairy, manlike figure about six feet tall, with large hands and feet, dark brown hair three to four inches long, and a flattened nose. One arm looks broken. One eye looks knocked from its socket, as if by a bullet from behind.

Hansen tells audiences it was found in Siberia and that he is only the caretaker for an eccentric California millionaire. Canada Customs once detains him on suspicion he is hauling a human cadaver. The FBI is told it might be a murder victim, but no investigation follows.

In April 1969, Argosy science editor Ivan T. Sanderson puts the Iceman on the magazine cover and asks whether this is the missing link between man and the apes. He contacts Smithsonian primatologist John Napier. Hansen then pulls the exhibit, saying the California owner ordered it withdrawn, and later puts a new Iceman on the road that observers call an obvious latex model.

Napier concludes Hansen had commissioned a West Coast company to make the figure in 1967, and that the original and the so-called substitute were the same carnival prop, repositioned and refrozen between shows. The Smithsonian is satisfied it is latex rubber and hair. In 2013 the sideshow gaff sells on eBay and ends up on display at the Museum of the Weird in Austin, Texas.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Iceman
posts.headline: Near Winona, Minnesota. Late 1960s.

posts.text:
Have you heard of Tartarus?

Top 5 things to know about the abyss where the fallen angels are chained:

1) In Greek mythology, Tartarus is the deep abyss used as a dungeon of torment for the wicked and as the prison of the Titans, and in Hesiod's Theogony it is one of the earliest beings to exist, alongside Chaos and Gaia.

2) In the Iliad, Zeus says Tartarus is "as far beneath Hades as heaven is above earth," and Hesiod says a bronze anvil falling from heaven would take nine days to reach earth and nine more to reach Tartarus.

3) Its prisoners included the Titans after they lost to the gods of Olympus, plus the Cyclopes and the hundred-armed Hecatonchires, and later myths filled it with mortals like Sisyphus, Tantalus and Ixion, each given a punishment to fit his crime.

4) In the Greek text of the Book of Enoch, dated to 400 to 200 BC, God places the archangel Uriel "in charge of the world and of Tartarus," generally understood as the place where 200 fallen Watchers are imprisoned.

5) The New Testament never uses the noun, but 2 Peter 2:4 uses a verb meaning "throw to Tartarus," saying God did not spare angels when they sinned but "cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment," and Jude 1:6 describes angels bound in chains under everlasting darkness.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tartarus
posts.headline: Have you heard of Tartarus?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Bermuda Triangle?

Top 5 things to know about the Devil's Triangle:

1) The Bermuda Triangle, also called the Devil's Triangle, is a loosely defined region of the North Atlantic roughly bounded by Florida, Bermuda and Puerto Rico, and the urban legend that ships and planes vanish there under mysterious circumstances dates only from the mid-20th century.

2) The earliest suggestion of unusual disappearances near Bermuda appeared in an article by Edward Van Winkle Jones of the Miami Herald, distributed by the Associated Press on September 17, 1950, and in 1952 Fate magazine's "Sea Mystery at Our Back Door" first laid out the now-familiar triangle.

3) The legend's centerpiece is Flight 19, five US Navy torpedo bombers lost on a training mission in December 1945, and a 1962 magazine article claimed the flight leader said, "We cannot be sure of any direction ... everything is wrong ... strange ... the ocean doesn't look as it should."

4) Vincent Gaddis popularized the idea in a 1964 Argosy article called "The Deadly Bermuda Triangle," later writers including Charles Berlitz in 1974 added supernatural elements, and they couldn't even agree on the boundaries, which ranged from 1.3 to 3.9 million square kilometers.

5) Researcher Larry Kusche's 1975 book The Bermuda Triangle Mystery: Solved concluded that the number of ships and aircraft lost there was not significantly greater than in any other part of the ocean, and Lloyd's of London and the US Coast Guard found no evidence of unusual activity either.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bermuda_Triangle
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Bermuda Triangle?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Golem?

Top 5 things to know about the clay giant of Jewish folklore:

1) A golem is an animated humanlike being in Jewish folklore made entirely from inanimate matter, usually clay or mud, and the word appears just once in the Bible, in Psalm 139, for the unfinished human being before God's eyes.

2) The Talmud says Adam himself was first a golem when his dust was kneaded into a shapeless husk, and the earliest known written account of how to create one comes from Eleazar of Worms in the late 12th and early 13th centuries.

3) In the tales, a golem is brought to life by writing the name of God on a slip of paper placed in its mouth or forehead, or by writing the Hebrew word emet, "truth," on its forehead, and erasing the first letter turns it into met, "dead."

4) The most famous golem is the one Rabbi Judah Loew of Prague supposedly made in the late 16th century from clay on the banks of the Vltava River to defend the Prague ghetto, called Josef or Yossele, whom he deactivated each Friday evening so it could rest on the Sabbath.

5) Legend says its body still lies in the attic of Prague's Old New Synagogue, though when the attic was renovated in 1883 no evidence of it was found, and historians generally view the Prague story as a German literary invention of the early 19th century.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golem
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Golem?

posts.text:
Have you heard of Area 51?

Top 5 things to know about the secret Nevada air base:

1) Area 51 is a highly classified US Air Force facility in southern Nevada, 83 miles north-northwest of Las Vegas, officially called Homey Airport or Groom Lake after the salt flat beside its airfield.

2) The CIA established the Groom Lake test site in April 1955 for Project AQUATONE, the Lockheed U-2 spy plane, and designer Kelly Johnson said that flying over it, "within thirty seconds, you knew that was the place."

3) The Air Force officially acknowledged the site's existence in 1998, and on June 25, 2013 the CIA released a history confirming the U-2 was tested there, in response to a Freedom of Information Act request filed in 2005.

4) Its UFO reputation partly came from its own aircraft, since the U-2 flew above 60,000 feet and airline pilots saw its silver wings catch the setting sun, and OXCART veterans said airline pilots cruising over Nevada at dusk would see the spy plane whiz by at 2,000-plus mph and think UFO, so Project Blue Book checked flight records to dismiss most of those reports.

5) Bob Lazar claimed in 1989 that he worked on alien spacecraft at an underground site called S-4 near Papoose Lake, and in July 2019 more than 2,000,000 people responded to a joke Facebook post to "Storm Area 51," though only between 1,500 and 3,000 people showed up at two nearby festivals and seven people were reportedly arrested.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_51
posts.headline: Have you heard of Area 51?

posts.text:
Have you heard of Sodom and Gomorrah?

Top 5 things to know about the cities of the plain destroyed in Genesis:

1) Sodom and Gomorrah were two of the "cities of the plain" in the story of Abraham and Lot, destroyed by God for their wickedness in Genesis 19:1-28, and the story parallels the Genesis flood narrative in its theme of God's anger at human sin.

2) Before the destruction, Abraham bargains with God, asking "Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?" and starting at 50 people, he gets God to agree to spare Sodom if ten righteous people can be found.

3) Two angels are welcomed into Lot's home and lead him, his wife and his two daughters out of the city, then God rains sulfur and fire on the plain, and Lot's wife, who ignores the warning and looks back, is turned into a pillar of salt.

4) Ezekiel 16:49-50 describes the iniquity of Sodom as "pride, fulness of bread, and careless ease" while the poor and needy went unhelped, and Deuteronomy, Isaiah and Jeremiah use the two cities as a byword for destruction and desolation.

5) The cities may have been based on real places along the Dead Sea, with sites like Bab edh-Dhra and Numeira suggested, and Strabo and Josephus both place Sodom near the Dead Sea, but the archaeological evidence is inconclusive.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodom_and_Gomorrah

posts.text:
Answer: A) Piasa Bird

The Piasa Bird is the name given to a monster mural painted by Native Americans high on a limestone bluff above the Mississippi River at present-day Alton, Illinois. French explorers Marquette and Jolliet described it in 1673 as a multicolored, human-faced creature with a long tail ending in a fish-like fin, and a copy of their sketch survives on 17th-century maps. The famous version with wings only turns up in 19th-century drawings, and folklorists doubt the popular legend of the chief Ouatoga who fended it off, tracing that tale to writer John Russell in 1836. The original bluff face was quarried away in the 1840s, a newer replica now stands in Alton, and several researchers believe the creature was the underwater panther of native lore.

How'd you do?

posts.text:
Durupınar Formation, eastern Türkiye, near Mount Ararat. Summer 2026.

High in the rugged country of eastern Türkiye, about 18 miles south of Mount Ararat, an enormous stone formation rises from the earth. From the air it looks like the remains of a great ship, pointed at one end, rounded at the other, and about 538 feet long. For generations, believers have asked whether it could be the final resting place of Noah's Ark. Genesis gives the Ark as 300 cubits long and 50 wide, and depending on how long you take a cubit to be, that lands remarkably close.

Turkish Army Captain Ilhan Durupinar noticed its outline in aerial photographs in 1959, and expeditions have followed ever since. Some claimed petrified wood, iron fasteners and giant anchor stones. Geologists answered that it's just folded rock and hardened mud, and in 1996 Lorence Collins and David Fasold, once an enthusiastic supporter of the Ark idea, concluded the same.

This summer, a team led by Professor Cenker Atila of Sivas Cumhuriyet University began the most extensive examination yet, with detailed 3D maps, GPS reference points and ground-penetrating radar. According to the university, the radar detected regularly angled cavities beneath the formation, and soil samples inside the boat-shaped outline carried about 40 percent more carbon than samples outside it.

The researchers have not announced the discovery of Noah's Ark. Core samples are still being studied, with fuller results expected in 2027.

Source: https://garnerreport.com/has-noahs-ark-left-a-shadow-beneath-the-earth/

posts.text:
White River, near Newport, Arkansas. July 1, 1915.

On July 1, 1915, the owner of a plantation near the White River in northeastern Arkansas sees something in the water. He says it has gray skin and is as wide as a car and three cars long. As the news spreads, folks start building a rope net to catch it, but the work stops when the money and materials run out.

In the first week of 1937, fishermen notice their catches have dropped, and the creature is spotted again. This time it's reported to plantation owner Bramlett Bateman, who later confirms it, describing skin like an elephant, four or five feet wide and twelve feet long, with the face of a catfish, lolling on the surface. Worried about his crops, he intends to blow up the eddy with TNT, but the authorities won't give him permission.

The story turns into a minor media sensation, and visitors pour in from across the country, some with cameras, some with explosives, and even a machine gun. A plan to net the creature fails, and a deep sea diver can't find it. Bateman ends up accused of a hoax, despite more than 100 recorded sightings.

In the summer of 1971, witnesses describe it as the size of a boxcar with a bone sticking out of its forehead, and others find three-toed tracks 14 inches long on Towhead Island. Then in 1973, the Arkansas legislature creates the White River Monster Refuge, where it's illegal to harm it. Locals just call it Whitey.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_River_Monster

posts.text:
Greenbrier County, West Virginia. January 23, 1897.

Zona Heaster Shue is found dead in her home not long after marrying a blacksmith named Edward Shue. A coroner's jury says heart disease, and she's buried the very next day.

Her mother, Mary Jane Heaster, doesn't believe it. She says Zona's spirit came to her and told her Edward had broken her neck. Mary spends hours in the prosecutor's office, and he finally orders an exhumation after the doctor admits he never made a complete examination.

On February 22, the autopsy runs three hours in a one-room schoolhouse. Zona's neck is broken and her windpipe is crushed, with finger marks on her throat. Edward is arrested, and it comes out that he has been married twice before, and that his second wife died under mysterious circumstances less than a year after their wedding.

At the trial that June, the prosecution stays away from the ghost, but the defense questions Mary about it for so long that she never wavers. Edward is convicted of first degree murder and sentenced to life, and he dies in prison in 1900.

Today a state historical marker near the cemetery where Zona is buried calls it the only known case in which testimony from a ghost helped convict a murderer.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenbrier_Ghost

posts.text:
Godman Army Airfield, Fort Knox, Kentucky. January 7, 1948.

Early that afternoon, at 1:15, Godman Field gets a call from the Kentucky Highway Patrol about an unusual aerial object near Maysville. Twenty minutes later, another call describes it as circular, 250 to 300 feet across, moving west at a pretty good clip. By about 1:45, the tower operators can see it for themselves, and they decide it is neither an aircraft nor a weather balloon.

Four Kentucky Air National Guard Mustangs are told to approach it, one flown by Captain Thomas Mantell, a 25-year-old World War II veteran who won the Distinguished Flying Cross towing a glider under heavy fire on D-Day. He climbs to 15,000 feet, then keeps going to 22,000. His wingmen don't follow because they don't have enough oxygen, and they try to get him to level off. His plane doesn't have the oxygen for that altitude either.

Past 25,000 feet, the Army later decides, Mantell blacks out. Witnesses see his Mustang spiraling down in a circle, and at 3:50 the tower hears it has crashed on a farm south of Franklin, on the Tennessee line.

Rumors spread about a saucer shooting him down or radioactive wreckage, and no evidence ever backs them up. In 1952, Project Blue Book decides he was chasing a top secret Skyhook balloon, but it's still remembered as one of the most publicized early UFO reports.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mantell_UFO_incident

posts.text:
Ape Canyon, Mount St. Helens, Washington. July 1924.

Marion Smith, his son and their partners have been prospecting a claim in the wilds at the foot of Mount St. Helens for six years, about eight miles from Spirit Lake. They've seen strange four-toed tracks there more than once, 13 to 14 inches long, with short, stubby toes almost square across.

Around sixteen days earlier, Smith and Fred Beck spot something peeking out from behind a tree about 100 yards away. They fire, and Smith thinks he hit it in the head. It falls back, but by the time they cross the canyon, it's gone.

Then on a Wednesday, Smith's son is walking back from the spring with only a revolver when something charges out of the alders, waving its arms over its head and striking its chest. He fires, and it comes within 15 feet before it turns back. The next day, he and Beck meet another one, and with Peterson running out of the cabin, the men fire sixteen shots between them. Beck's last shot seems to hit it, and it topples over the edge of a canyon too steep to climb down without ropes.

That night around eleven, rocks start falling through the hole in the cabin roof. The bombardment lasts until after two while the creatures shove at the door and drum on their chests. The men build a big fire, nail the door shut, and in the morning start home to Kelso.

All that week hunters comb the woods and report nothing. Plenty of people in Kelso call it imagination. The miners insist they saw them. The place is known as Ape Canyon today.

Source: https://twrps.com/history/news-from-the-past/bigfoot/

posts.text:
Have you heard of Momo the Missouri Monster?

Top 5 things to know about the hairy creature reported around Louisiana, Missouri, in 1972:

1) Momo is a large, hairy humanoid said to have been sighted in rural Missouri, described as a human or upright ape about 7 feet tall, covered in dark hair and giving off a putrid odor.

2) On July 11, 1972, two young boys were playing in their backyard on the rural outskirts of Louisiana, Missouri, when their older sister Doris heard them screaming from the kitchen.

3) Looking out the window, she said she saw a massive, dark-haired, man-like creature holding what appeared to be a dead dog, with a "pumpkin-shaped head" and large glowing orange eyes.

4) More sightings followed that year, including one from the local fire chief and city council member Richard Allan Murray, who said a massive upright creature showed up in his headlights along a creek bed, and a 20-person posse went out to hunt it with no luck.

5) Unlike the Fouke Monster or the Honey Island Swamp monster, Momo never became a big tourist draw, but Six Flags St. Louis ran a ride named after it from 1973 to 1994, and the 2019 docudrama Momo: The Missouri Monster features Cliff Barackman and James "Bobo" Fay of Finding Bigfoot.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Momo_the_Monster

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Flying Dutchman?

Top 5 things to know about the ghost ship doomed to sail forever:

1) The Flying Dutchman is a legendary ghost ship that can never make port and is doomed to sail the sea forever, and the stories likely began in the 17th-century golden age of the Dutch East India Company.

2) The first known print reference comes from John MacDonald in 1790, who wrote that sailors in a storm said they saw it, a Dutch ship that came to the Cape in bad weather, couldn't get a pilot into harbour and was lost, and has appeared in storms ever since.

3) An 1821 story in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine names the captain Van der Decken, who swore he would round the Cape of Good Hope even if he had to beat about "till the day of judgment," and says the crew tries to hand passing ships letters addressed to people long dead, which bring misfortune if accepted.

4) In ocean lore, seeing it is a portent of doom, Sir Walter Scott called it "the worst of all possible omens," and the most likely real explanation is a superior mirage, or Fata Morgana, that makes a distant ship appear to float in the air.

5) At 4 a.m. on July 11, 1881, off the coast of Australia, a log from the royal voyage of the future King George V records the Flying Dutchman crossing their bows in "a strange red light," with 13 people seeing it, and later that morning the seaman who first reported it fell from the rigging and was killed.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_Dutchman
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Flying Dutchman?

posts.text:
Have you heard of Project Blue Book?

Top 5 things to know about the Air Force's official UFO investigation:

1) Project Blue Book was the US Air Force's systematic study of UFOs, running from March 1952 until it was shut down on December 17, 1969, and headquartered at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio.

2) It followed Project Sign in 1947 and Project Grudge in 1949, and its first director, Captain Edward J. Ruppelt, officially coined the term "unidentified flying object" to replace phrases like "flying saucer" and "flying disk."

3) The name came from the blue booklets used for college exams, because all the attention from high-ranking officers made the project feel as important as a final exam.

4) Astronomer J. Allen Hynek was its scientific consultant right up to the end, created the categories now known as close encounters, and started out a pronounced skeptic but moved to a more wavering skepticism after running into a minority of reports he thought were unexplainable.

5) By the time it ended, Blue Book had collected 12,618 UFO reports, and while most were put down to natural phenomena or conventional aircraft, 701 stayed unexplained even after stringent analysis.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Blue_Book
posts.headline: Have you heard of Project Blue Book?

posts.text:
Have you heard of Black Shuck?

Top 5 things to know about the phantom black dog of East Anglia:

1) Black Shuck, also called Old Shuck or Old Shock, is a ghostly black dog said to roam the coastline and countryside of Norfolk, Suffolk, the Cambridgeshire Fens and Essex, and the name may come from the Old English scucca, meaning "devil" or "fiend."

2) Descriptions range from a large dog to the size of a calf or a horse, and in 1850 Reverend E. S. Taylor wrote of people who had seen "a black shaggy dog, with fiery eyes and of immense size, and who visits churchyards at midnight."

3) In 1901 W. A. Dutt wrote that his footfalls make no sound, that he has one fiery eye in the middle of his head like a Cyclops, and that meeting him can be a warning you will die before the end of the year, though other tales call him companionable.

4) On August 4, 1577, during a violent storm, Abraham Fleming's pamphlet A Straunge and Terrible Wunder says a black dog, "or the divel in such a likenesse," ran down St Mary's Church in Bungay, Suffolk, and wrung the necks of two people kneeling in prayer.

5) That same morning lightning struck Holy Trinity Church in Blythburgh during the service and a man and a boy were found dead, and the scorch marks on its north door, blamed on Shuck and known as the devil's fingerprints, can still be seen today.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Shuck

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Ophanim?

Top 5 things to know about the wheels full of eyes in Ezekiel's vision:

1) The name comes from the Hebrew word for "wheels," and they are also called galgalim, meaning "spheres, wheels, whirlwinds," after the wheels Ezekiel sees beside the chariot of God in Ezekiel 1:15-21.

2) In the vision there are four wheels, each made of two nested wheels, moving alongside the winged cherubim beneath the throne of God, and "their rims were full of eyes round about."

3) The wheels go wherever the cherubim go because the spirit of the cherubim is in them, and since a chariot wheel can only roll forward or back, two wheels crossed together could move instantly in any of the four directions.

4) One of the Dead Sea Scrolls, 4Q405, treats them as angels, late sections of the Book of Enoch make them celestial beings who never sleep and guard the throne of God alongside the cherubim and seraphim, and the Second Book of Enoch calls them the "many-eyed ones."

5) Maimonides ranks the ophanim second closest to God among the angels, Jewish morning prayer still says "the ophanim and the holy living creatures" rise up to praise God, and some Christian traditions identify them with the Thrones.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ophanim

posts.text:
Answer: B) Hoop Snake

The hoop snake is a legendary creature of the United States, Canada and Australia that grabs its tail in its jaws like the ouroboros and rolls after its prey like a wheel, and in one version it straightens out at the last second to strike with its venomous tail, so the only escape is to hide behind a tree, which takes the blow and promptly dies from the poison. It turns up in a letter from 1784, long before the Pecos Bill stories made it famous, and in the folklore of Virginia and West Virginia, with alleged sightings from the St. Croix River valley to Prince Edward Island. Science has never accepted it, and naturalist Raymond Ditmars once put $10,000 in trust at a New York bank for the first person who could bring him evidence of one.

How'd you do?

posts.text:
Stub Newell's farm, Cardiff, New York. October 16, 1869.

Two men, Gideon Emmons and Henry Nichols, are digging a well behind William C. "Stub" Newell's barn when they uncover a giant. A stone man more than ten feet long, roughly 3,000 pounds, lying in the dirt like he's been there for ages. One of them reportedly says, "I declare, some old Indian has been buried here!"

The first day, people look for free. The next day, Newell puts up a tent and charges 50 cents for 15 minutes, and soon three to five hundred people a day are rolling in by wagon and carriage. Some say it's an old statue. Plenty believe it's a petrified man, one of the giants of Genesis 6:4: "There were giants in the earth in those days." Some preachers even defend it.

It was a setup from the start. George Hull, a New York tobacconist and Newell's cousin, had lost an argument at a Methodist revival meeting over that very verse. Angry, he set out to prove how easily people could be fooled. In 1868 he had a block of gypsum quarried in Fort Dodge, Iowa, telling the workers it was for a monument to Abraham Lincoln, and had it carved in Chicago in his own likeness, with quilts hung up to muffle the sound. He stained it, rubbed it with acid, beat it with needles to fake pores, shipped it by rail, and buried it on Newell's farm one night in November 1868.

Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh points out it's made of soluble gypsum with fresh tool marks still on it, and calls it "a most decided humbug." Nobody cares. Hull sells his share for $23,000, and when the new owners turn down P. T. Barnum's $50,000 offer, Barnum has a copy made and claims his is the real one. That's when owner David Hannum is quoted saying, "There's a sucker born every minute." It's been blamed on Barnum ever since.

Hull confesses to the press on December 10, 1869. Both giants are still on display today, the original in Cooperstown, New York.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiff_Giant
posts.headline: Stub Newell's farm, Cardiff, New York. October 16, 1869.

posts.text:
Love Point, Kent Island, Maryland. May 31, 1982.

For years, people around the Chesapeake Bay have been describing the same thing. Something long, dark and snakelike, 25 to 40 feet long and only eight to ten inches thick, with a football-shaped head and no fins at all. The papers call it Chessie.

On Memorial Day 1982, Robert Frew and his wife Karen are having a holiday meal with family and friends at their home on Love Point, looking out over the bay. Around 7:30 in the evening, someone notices a large object about 100 feet offshore, moving against the tide.

Frew grabs his binoculars. It's a long, dark, humped creature, swimming lazily along. So he loads a tape into his video camera and starts rolling, and you can hear his kids squealing in the background as it passes near some swimmers. The witnesses put it at about 30 feet long and about 10 inches wide.

That August, researchers from a Baltimore group called the Enigma Project get the tape in front of Dr. George Zug and other scientists at the Smithsonian's Museum of Natural History. They're intrigued, but the tape just isn't clear enough for them to say what the animate object is. The Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory offers to run computer enhancement, and it pulls an unmistakable serpentine shape out of the water. Then the funding runs out, and since 1983 the tape has sat in limbo.

Asked if it might have been a turtle, Karen Frew has a short answer. "What I saw was no turtle."

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chessie_(sea_monster)
posts.headline: Love Point, Kent Island, Maryland. May 31, 1982.

posts.text:
The Stanley Hotel, Estes Park, Colorado. Opened July 4, 1909.

In 1903, steam-car inventor Freelan Oscar Stanley comes to Colorado with a life-threatening case of tuberculosis, and the mountain air around Estes Park brings him back. So he builds a grand hotel there, about five miles from what's now the entrance to Rocky Mountain National Park, and opens it on July 4, 1909. It's said to be one of the few hotels in the world running entirely on electricity.

There isn't enough power, so in June 1911 the hotel puts in a backup gas lighting system. On June 25, the day after the pipes are filled, there's an explosion. Part of the building is wrecked, eight people are hurt, and the Associated Press reports a hotel worker named Elizabeth Wilson with both ankles broken.

The way the hotel's ghost story tells it, it happened in Room 217. Head chambermaid Elizabeth Wilson walks into the room and lights a candle, and leaking gas blows it apart, hard enough that a bathtub is said to have gone flying. She survives and goes back to work at the Stanley. But after she dies, guests in 217 start waking up to a room cleaner than they left it, their clothes folded and their suitcases organized. Unmarried couples say something cold slips into bed beside them while they sleep.

In 1974, Stephen King and his wife Tabitha check in for one night, just as the hotel is closing for the winter, and find themselves the only guests in all those long, empty corridors. Room 217 is said to be the one King got. That night he dreams of his three-year-old son running through the halls, looking back over his shoulder and screaming. He gets up, lights a cigarette at the window, and by the time it's done, he has the bones of The Shining.

Guests still report children laughing and running on the fourth floor with nobody there, F. O. Stanley in the billiards room and bar, and his wife Flora in the piano room. Ghost Hunters and Ghost Adventures have both come calling, and it's now considered one of America's most haunted hotels.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Stanley_Hotel
posts.headline: The Stanley Hotel, Estes Park, Colorado. Opened July 4, 1909.

posts.text:
Pantex Plant, northeast of Amarillo, Texas. September 1, 2015.

Pantex is where America assembles and takes apart its nuclear weapons. At 7:08 in the morning, the plant's ground surveillance radar picks up something about a mile and three quarters southwest of a secured area, moving north at only 10 to 15 miles per hour.

Security kicks into its drone response plan. Gates into the protected areas get locked down and armed patrols move into defensive positions.

A lieutenant and a security officer chase it up Pantex Drive, trying to get right underneath it, but they can't catch up. So they stop, get out, and study it through binoculars. No sound. No wings. No propeller or rotor. Nothing they can see holding it up.

Another team tracks it for three to five minutes with a camera mounted on a BearCat armored vehicle. They put it 100 to 200 feet up, about four feet tall and two feet wide at the bottom, tapering to a rounded top, like a diamond. Some officers see black. Others see silver, red and blue.

They follow it for miles off the property as it seems to speed up and change direction, and finally lose it near County Road G, heading east-northeast. Sandia National Laboratories enhances the tower video, and the whole file goes to the FBI. The newly released report never says what it was.

Source: https://garnerreport.com/ufo-alert-at-pantex/
posts.headline: Pantex Plant, northeast of Amarillo, Texas. September 1, 2015.

posts.text:
Bluff Creek, Six Rivers National Forest, Northern California. October 20, 1967.

Roger Patterson and Bob Gimlin are two former rodeo riders who have hauled three horses deep into Bigfoot country, where people have been finding giant footprints since 1958. Gimlin isn't even sure the thing exists, but he goes along with the one thing Patterson insists on. Nobody shoots it.

Early that Friday afternoon, somewhere between 1:15 and 1:40, they're riding up the creek when they round an overturned tree with a root ball almost as tall as a room. Behind a logjam left over from the flood of '64, there it is. A big, hairy, upright figure on the far bank.

Patterson's horse rears. He fights his way out of the saddle, digs the camera out of his saddlebag and runs at it, filming the whole way. At about 80 feet, the figure glances back over its right shoulder, and Patterson drops to his knees. He later says the look on its face was contempt and disgust.

It walks off into the trees just as the reel runs out. The whole encounter lasts less than two minutes. They track it until they lose it in heavy brush, then come back with plaster and cast two of its footprints.

Patterson said the creature on that film was real right up until he died in 1972. Gimlin has always denied any part in a hoax. About a minute of shaky film, and people are still arguing over every frame.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patterson%E2%80%93Gimlin_film
posts.headline: Bluff Creek, Six Rivers National Forest, Northern California. October 20, 1967.

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Si-Te-Cah?

Top 5 things to know about the red-haired giants of Lovelock Cave:

1) According to reports of Northern Paiute oral history, the Si-Te-Cah were a legendary tribe the Paiutes fought and eventually wiped out or drove away, with the final battle at what is now Lovelock Cave near Lovelock, Nevada.

2) The name means "tule-eaters" in Northern Paiute, and to escape the Paiutes they were said to live on rafts made of tule, a fibrous water plant, on Lake Humboldt.

3) They were said to have red hair and are sometimes described as cannibals, and in 1883 Sarah Winnemucca, daughter of Chief Winnemucca, wrote that her family kept some of their reddish hair, handed down from father to son, trimming a mourning dress.

4) In 1911, guano miners digging in Lovelock Cave found mummified remains and artifacts under 3 to 6 feet of guano, miner James H. Hart described a mummified man 6 feet 6 inches tall with "distinctly red" hair, and the best adult mummy was later boiled and destroyed by a local fraternal lodge that wanted the skeleton for initiations.

5) Only some later versions make them giants, and Adrienne Mayor suggests that idea started with tourist displays, that the skeletons were normal size, and that ancient dark hair can turn rusty red after death.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Si-Te-Cah
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Si-Te-Cah?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Banshee?

Top 5 things to know about the wailing woman of Irish folklore:

1) The name comes from the Irish bean sí, from Old Irish ben síde, meaning "woman of the fairy mound," after the ancient mounds that dot the Irish countryside.

2) She is a female spirit who heralds the death of a family member by screaming, wailing, shrieking or keening, and her cry could be a household's first warning, even when someone had died far away and the news hadn't arrived yet.

3) Descriptions vary: long streaming hair that she may be seen combing, a grey cloak over a green dress, and eyes red from weeping, and most tales that mention her height make her short, between one and four feet tall.

4) Tradition says she laments only certain old Irish families, mostly surnames beginning with Ó or Mac, and the Ua Briain banshee, Aibell, was said to rule 25 other banshees, while several appearing at once meant the death of someone great or holy.

5) Accounts reach back as far as 1380, in parts of Leinster her wail is said to be so piercing it can shatter glass, and in Scotland a similar spirit, the bean nighe, is seen washing the bloodstained clothes of those about to die.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banshee
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Banshee?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Men in Black?

Top 5 things to know about the strangers who show up after a UFO sighting:

1) In UFO lore, men in black are said to be agents in dark suits who question, intimidate, harass and threaten UFO witnesses to keep them quiet about what they saw.

2) They are typically described as tall men with expressionless faces and slightly pale skin, wearing black suits and black sunglasses, and the term covers any strange or threatening person whose arrival can be linked to a UFO sighting.

3) One of the earliest stories dates to 1947, when Harold Dahl claimed a man in a dark suit warned him not to discuss his alleged UFO sighting on Maury Island.

4) In the mid-1950s, ufologist Albert K. Bender claimed men in dark suits visited and warned him to stop investigating UFOs, and John Keel, author of The Mothman Prophecies, called them "demonic supernaturals."

5) Not every story holds up: Keel wrote that he was once mistaken for an MIB himself in 1967 while looking for a phone to call a tow truck, and the legend went on to inspire the 1997 Men in Black film starring Will Smith and Tommy Lee Jones.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Men_in_black
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Men in Black?

posts.text:
Have you heard of Abaddon?

Top 5 things to know about the angel of the bottomless pit in Revelation:

1) Abaddon is a Hebrew word meaning "destruction" or "doom," its Greek counterpart Apollyon means "Destroyer," and the Bible uses it both for a place of destruction and for an angel of the abyss.

2) In the Hebrew Bible the word appears six times, in Job, Psalms and Proverbs, usually alongside Sheol, the resting place of the dead, as in Proverbs 27:20: "Sheol and Abaddon cannot be satisfied."

3) Revelation 9:11 gives the first known depiction of Abaddon as an individual instead of a place: a king, the angel of the bottomless pit, "whose name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek Apollyon."

4) He is king over a plague of locusts that look like horses with crowned human faces, women's hair, lions' teeth, wings, iron breastplates and scorpion tails, sent to torment for five months anyone without the seal of God on their foreheads.

5) Who he really is stays open to debate: Matthew Henry saw the Antichrist, other commentators identified him as Satan, The Interpreter's Bible calls him an angel of God carrying out destruction at God's bidding, and in The Pilgrim's Progress, Christian fights Apollyon for over half a day.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abaddon
posts.headline: Have you heard of Abaddon?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Rougarou?

Top 5 things to know about the werewolf of the Louisiana swamps:

1) The rougarou, also spelled roux-ga-roux, rugaroo or rugaru, is a legendary creature of Cajun and Creole folklore, and its name is a variant of the French loup-garou, meaning werewolf.

2) In Cajun and Creole legend it prowls the swamps around Acadiana and Greater New Orleans, along with the sugar cane fields and woodlands, and it is most often described as having a human body and the head of a wolf or dog.

3) Elders used the stories to scare children into behaving, and one version says the beast hunts down Catholics who don't follow the rules of Lent, echoing old French tales that breaking Lent seven years in a row turns you into a werewolf.

4) A common legend says the curse lasts 101 days and passes to a new person when the rougarou draws their blood, and some believe placing 13 small objects by the door keeps it away, because it is too simple-minded to count past 12.

5) Among the Ojibwe, rugaru is the name for a hairy man who appears as a sign of danger in the community, and author Peter Matthiessen suggested the word may come from the loup-garou of French Canadian trappers.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rougarou
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Rougarou?

Answer: D) Kongamato

The kongamato, whose name means "overwhelmer of boats," is a pterosaur-like cryptid reported from the Jiundu Swamp in the Mwinilunga district of western Zambia, and from Angola and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Frank Melland wrote about it in his 1923 book In Witch-Bound Africa, describing a reddish flier with a 4 to 7 foot wingspan said to capsize boats from below, and Kaonde people shown a pterosaur picture in his book said it looked exactly like one. Accounts add smooth featherless skin and a toothy beak, while skeptics point to shoebill or saddle-billed storks and Ivan T. Sanderson favored a giant bat.

How'd you do?

posts.text:
Route 150, Kensington, New Hampshire, about three miles south of Exeter. September 3, 1965.

It's around 2 in the morning, and 18-year-old Norman Muscarello is walking home along the highway. He's three weeks away from leaving for the Navy, he's just sold his car, and he's been hitchhiking back from his girlfriend's house in Amesbury, Massachusetts. At that hour there's hardly any traffic.

Then he sees five bright red lights flashing in the distance. At first he figures it's a police car or a fire engine. It isn't. The lights are hovering just above the trees, bathing a field and two houses in brilliant red. He puts the object at 80 to 90 feet across, and it makes absolutely no sound. When it starts moving toward him, he dives into a ditch. He pounds on a farmhouse door yelling for help, and the family inside later admits they heard him but were too frightened to open it.

He flags down a car and gets a ride to the Exeter police station, pale and shaking. Officer Eugene Bertrand drives him back out. Earlier that night, Bertrand had stopped for a frightened woman who said a huge object with flashing red lights had followed her car for about 12 miles.

Out in the field, horses start neighing and kicking the barn, dogs bark and howl, and an object rises slowly from the trees. Bertrand calls it a huge dark object "as big as a barn," with red lights flashing in sequence as it rocks back and forth. He drops to one knee and draws his revolver, then thinks better of it. Officer David Hunt arrives and watches it too. When a B-47 bomber flies over soon after, Hunt says there was no comparison.

The Pentagon blames stars and planets twinkling in a temperature inversion. The officers push back, and in January 1966 the Air Force writes that it has been unable to identify the object. Skeptics later suggested a KC-97 refueling tanker, but Muscarello insisted for the rest of his life that what he saw was real.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exeter_incident
posts.headline: Route 150, Kensington, New Hampshire, about three miles south of Exeter. September 3, 1965.

posts.text:
Bladenboro, Bladen County, North Carolina. December 1953 to January 1954.

On December 29, 1953, something kills a dog in Clarkton, about eight miles from Bladenboro. Witnesses describe the animal as sleek, black, and about five feet long.

Two nights later, on New Year's Eve, two dogs belonging to a Bladenboro resident are found dead near their kennels, "torn into ribbons and crushed." The owner says it killed one dog at 10:30, then came back and carried the body off, and at 1:30 in the morning it came back again for the other one.

More dogs die over the next week. A pet rabbit turns up cleanly decapitated, and a goat is found with its head flattened. When one dog is autopsied, it reportedly has barely two or three drops of blood left in it, and the newspapers start calling it a vampire beast.

Nobody can agree on what it is. One local says it had a face exactly like a cat, only bigger than any cat he'd ever seen, with a long tail. Others compare it to a bear or a panther. A boy says it made a noise like a baby crying on his porch. On January 5, a woman says "a big mountain lion" ran straight at her and only turned away when she screamed. Hunters from Wilmington track it three miles around the swamp and find claw prints at least an inch long, and along a creek bank there are two sets of tracks, one smaller, like it has a mate or young nearby.

By January 6, more than 800 people with guns and dogs are combing the swamps, and officials shut the hunt down as too dangerous. On January 13, a farmer shoots a bobcat caught in a steel trap in Big Swamp, and Mayor Woodrow Fussell announces the beast is dead. Plenty of people doubt a bobcat could have done all that. Fussell, who ran the town theater and booked a movie called The Big Cat right in the middle of the scare, later said he thought it was a hoax and that "a little publicity never hurts a town."

Bladenboro still holds a Beast Fest every year, with the beast as its mascot.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beast_of_Bladenboro
posts.headline: Bladenboro, Bladen County, North Carolina. December 1953 to January 1954.

posts.text:
Whaley House, San Diego Avenue, Old Town San Diego, California. Built 1857.

In 1852, a man named James "Yankee Jim" Robinson is convicted of attempted grand larceny for trying to steal a boat, and he's hanged from a gallows off the back of a wagon on this very lot. One of the people watching that day is a merchant named Thomas Whaley. A few years later, he buys the land anyway.

Whaley designs a two-story brick Greek Revival house, the oldest brick structure in Southern California, and moves his family in on August 22, 1857. According to the San Diego Union, soon after they move in, heavy footsteps start moving through the house. Whaley says they sound like the boots of a large man, and he finally decides they belong to Yankee Jim.

The house sees plenty of grief. Baby Thomas Jr. dies of scarlet fever at 18 months. Daughter Violet, heartbroken after a disastrous marriage, dies by suicide in 1885 at just 22. Youngest daughter Lillian lives there until her death in 1953, convinced Yankee Jim never left.

Visitors and staff still report glimpses of the Whaleys themselves: Thomas on the upper landing in a frock coat and pantaloons, his face turned away, and Anna in the downstairs rooms and the garden. In 1964, Regis Philbin, filming for a local San Diego morning show, says he noticed "something filmy white" on the wall. He flipped on his flashlight and found nothing but a portrait of Anna Whaley. Years later he still said, "there was something going on in that house."

Travel Channel's America's Most Haunted went further, calling it the most supernatural home in the United States.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whaley_House_(San_Diego,_California)
posts.headline: Whaley House, San Diego Avenue, Old Town San Diego, California. Built 1857.

Lakewood, Colorado, just west of Denver. September 8, 2026.

It's about 7:05 in the evening and a Lakewood resident is sitting outside, just watching the clouds. Then they notice something that doesn't feel right. The birds and the animals around them have gone unusually quiet.

A bright object appears in the southern sky, almost like it's settling into view, and starts moving north. The witness gets it on video. It looks silver, metallic, but parts of it seem to turn see-through, and at other moments it looks less like a craft and more like a bright light. Even its shape won't hold still.

It glides smoothly at changing speeds, no zigzags, no sudden turns, and there's no sound at all. No engine, no propeller, nothing. They put it at bigger than an airliner.

Then, about thirty seconds in, it's just gone. It doesn't slip behind a cloud. It doesn't fade off into the distance. It simply stops being there.

The witness files the whole thing with the National UFO Reporting Center as sighting 200790, footage and all, and that strange silence before it showed up is the one detail they made sure to include.

Source: https://garnerreport.com/the-vanishing-object-over-lakewood/
posts.headline: Lakewood, Colorado, just west of Denver. September 8, 2026.
